content:
<Rep. Bennie G. Thompson>: Committee Democrats support ending the diversion of the 9/ 11 Passenger Security Fee (PSF) and ensuring Congress uses taxpayer dollars and fee revenues to make smart investments in the Transportation Security Administration's (TSA) personnel and screening technologies to keep the traveling public secure. For years, only a small amount of the PSF revenues have actually been used to fund TSA screening technology, while large portions of the revenue have gone to the General Fund of the Treasury for deficit reduction and the remaining collections have been used to offset the TSA Operations and Support (O&S) appropriation on a dollar-for-dollar basis.
Ending the fee diversion is a bipartisan policy objective, and Congress already made strides to that effect by enacting section 1940 of the TSA Modernization Act (Pub. L. 115-254), which ends the fee diversion on October 1, 2027. Existing law also establishes that all PSF collections shall be credited as offsetting collections--in other words, a substitute rather than supplement for general appropriations. H.R. 8770, the ``SAFEGUARDS Act,'' fails to advance the goal of ending fee diversions by, for example, making the implementation date sooner. This bill does not actually end the PSF diversion to General Fund of the Treasury since it does not change the relevant law. Instead, the legislation seeks to only express Congress' wish to end the diversion of the PSF, which was already accomplished by the TSA Modernization Act.
Moreover, H.R. 8770 does not raise additional revenue or increase TSA's overall budget. Instead, the bill would direct $750 million in annual funding generated by the PSF toward TSA technology procurements--$500 million towards checked baggage technology and $250 million towards checkpoint technology-- starting in Fiscal Year (FY) 2028. To be clear, this is simply a reapportionment of funds that would otherwise be credited as offsetting collections to TSA's O&S appropriation. Committee Democrats are concerned that the bill creates a large, unpaid-for hole in TSA's O&S appropriation, most of which goes to paying TSA workforce salaries and benefits. The bill would create a large appropriations shortfall and does nothing to provide a solution. Bringing PSF collections back to TSA, as will already occur under existing law, does not mean the agency's top-line budget will increase, since the fees are treated as offsetting collections by law. To pay for these large investments, appropriators would be faced with a choice to either increase TSA's overall budget or pull money from TSA workforce funding, leading to large staffing cuts.
Committee Democrats are committed to pursuing investments in next-generation technology to ensure the TSA workforce has the latest and greatest security tools at their disposal to keep Americans safe and secure. However, at a time when the Trump administration is attempting to privatize TSA and dismantle collective bargaining rights for frontline Transportation Security Officers, Congress must ensure efforts to increase technology funding do not lead to workforce cuts and, as a result, longer passenger checkpoint wait times and degraded passenger security. Committee Democrats will continue to work to ensure PSF diversions end as scheduled under existing statute and to increase technology funding while preventing negative impacts to the TSA workforce we rely on to keep the traveling public safe. If H.R. 8770 is enacted, Committee Democrats are committed to working with appropriators to ensure the bill will not result in workforce cuts.
Bennie G. Thompson.
